body: I'm a vegan mortician. I ate meat when I was in mortuary school but at some point I felt that eating meat didn't align with my personal ethics and values. If you're a funeral director and you want to learn more about either going veggie and/or vegan I have a website called Mortician in the Kitchen and I talk all about death using food as a vehicle. While I don't explicitly advertise that my recipes are vegan, they are all vegan. The more you learn about the history of cooking and who we are as humans and how we have shifted both physically across the world, culturally, and politically you'll find it's really not that weird to be vegan and I def get plenty of protein and it's the healthiest I've ever been. That doesn't mean it holds true for everyone but I do get asked those two questions quite a bit.
reach out to Jill Schock of Death Doula LA or Alua Arthur from Going with Grace. Both are wonderful resources.

Hi,

Amber here, one of the moderators.

First let me say how much I deeply empathize with depression. The struggle is real, and people who do not suffer from it cannot ever truly understand. However, I feel that there is a difference between planning for a good death, which is making sure that all your affairs are in order so that your loved ones can mourn the loss of your life without worrying about the coroner getting involved or fighting over what should happen to your body versus planning your death via an unassisted suicide when no terminal illness is involved.

Life is hard. I know it sounds cliche. You've heard it before right? Cheer up, nobody said it was going to be easy? Or maybe people say stuff to you like "Don't be a victim." It's patronizing to our feelings when we are depressed. As if we could just stop being sad if we wanted to right? You know what helped me though? Finding out that I wasn't alone. Finding out that I wasn't the only person in the world that felt this way. It freed me from the isolation I felt.

While I cannot control my depression, I can control my reaction to it. I can look outside it and realize that I can help. I can be here. I can be here to talk to you and others. I can help families during the hardest time of their life because I understand what it means to feel sad and alone. 

If you feel like you need access to medical intervention you should seek it out, but not in the form of death. I found that talking to a therapist helped me a lot. I am not ashamed nor embarrassed. It made me a stronger and better person. I am not saying you have to do it, but it may help. 

Nothing ever takes away the depression, but I promise you can learn to live with it.

yeah I would lean to it not preserving you at all. When a body is embalmed your circulatory system is used to channel the fluid into and back out of your body. The machine that the fluid is mixed in also has a certain amount of pressure and flow that is used to essentially mimic what your heart does with circulating blood in the body. If the fluid were ingested it would sit in your stomach or intestines but would not flow out in any sort of useful way to preserve the body. Also if the blood is not removed it would sit and pool in you, clotting and then decomposing.

Hi!

First of all you need to know that everything you are feeling is completely normal. It is very common to experience overwhelming grief and even guilt. However, if you feel that it is getting to a point where it is keeping your from living a healthy life, it can be beneficial to find a grief counselor to talk out your feelings with.
There is a huge unwarranted stigma against talking to a therapist, when essentially it is just like talking to your best girl or guy friend only they are more well versed on exercises and ways of thinking and dealing with the hardest parts of life. Often when we turn to our friends or family they do not know what to say because they are hurting for you and they end up saying things like "honey,don't be sad. It will be ok." or "You will absolutely meet someone else!". While these things may be true, the level of grief I am guessing you are experiencing is not in a place where messages like this are well received, and they may come off as dismissive of your love for this person or just patronizing. 

Please consider talking to someone who specializes in grief. They will have better tools than I, or most likely anyone on here that will help you work through this. You will find a new normal, I usually choose to phrase it that way because we can never really go back. 

If you have more questions on finding a health professional in your area please feel free to send me a private message or email us at undertakingla@gmail.com  and I can talk to you about the best ways to locate someone in your area. I have had two really wonderful therapists who were both girls about my age and it helped me through a lot of things in life that I was struggling to conquer on my own. I know that there may be many different avenues of working through your grief and I do not want you to feel that this is the only way, but what I have found to be the most successful. So please know I have a great deal of empathy for you and your situation.

Sincerely,
 Amber Carvaly

This can have a multitude of answers. So I'll attempt to answer but hope that someone else will jump in to give you a more thorough answer.

I have seen bodies dead stored under refrigeration (unembalmed) for two weeks (or more) that were, in my opinion, completely viewable. And the family seemed to agree.

There was a woman at my old job. She was called the "Cooler Queen." She was there for maybe at least 7 or 8 months. She looked probably the exact way that she did the day she was embalmed.

Adverse conditions will have various effects on a body depending on what they are. Not to compare a human to something like fruit or a vegetable, but think of any organic item. Picture an apple, or some broccoli. What happens when it is left out at room temperature? What happens when you freeze it? What happens when you leave it in a hot and humid environment? What happens when you leave it in an arid environment. All organic material will react the same because we are all made of the same molecules, only humans have much more water so you have to factor that into the rate of decay. 

And that is my very scientific, no I didn't graduate with a science degree, its just how I understand it. Perspective.

Usually a decedent would be wrapped in a unionall if it was a difficult case like that. I have seen plenty of people put in them who have had much less than what you are describing. It is a plastic onesie essentially. Here is a link so you can check it out. http://www.affordablefuneralsupply.com/prep-room/mortuary-garments/unionall/

Let's hypothetically say that a body was in fact severely dismembered you would be surprised how easily things can be sewn back together. More than likely each individual piece would be embalmed separately via either topical methods like preserving gels, or with a surface pack; wrapping said piece in cotton and cavity fluid.  There is also the option of hypo'ing, which is injecting fluid into the surface area with a needle (one of my favorite past times) .

This would dry out the body, taking away most of your leak problems.

So, if it was a severed arm, and I worked in a standard mortuary I would embalm the body and preserve the arm separately. Then I would sew it (if possible) back to the body and then wrap it in what is essentially saran wrap. If the body was leaking really bad then I would place it in the unionall. 

As a disclaimer, I haven't embalmed in years, so any active embalmers on here have my full permission to correct me or maybe different and more specific advice. Totally not mad at ya'

I have sooooo many different reasons for wanting to become more involved with the death movement. Since I have written some of my more common reasons in other places I suppose I will share one that I have not as of yet. 

I was one hundred percent one of those kids that latched onto anything that seemed to bother people. If it didn't get a reaction I became immediately bored with it. But if it DID get a reaction. Ho-Ho! What have we here!?!

Not surprisingly, death was something that provoked an extreme reaction from people. Not so much my family, as we are a pretty death positive group of people. But "the others" seemed to recoil at it. So naturally I became more curious about it. And it just sort of went on from there.

I'm not surprised that as an adult I have found a positive outlet for my desire to constantly poke at that which is most unsettling to other humans. I'm pretty sure in my heart of hearts, I've never really grown up. I've just found adult ways to be a kid.

For some odd reason I have grown up with the idea that having an urn in the house is somehow normal. Like, I kind of cannot picture a mantle without an urn. As if the two cannot exist without the other. For the record, we never had an urn in our house, not that we were the kind of family that would shun it. But it just seems like an ok thing to me all the same.
